mainTopic: אביי's two-part explanation of the broken-jug מחלוקת (stumbling during the fall, giving up the pieces after it), applied to the משנה, the ברייתא's camel, and רבי אלעזר's statement
overview: The amud opens with the end of a ברייתא: the חכמים say the man who broke his jug is exempt in human court but liable before Heaven. The ברייתא adds that everyone agrees a usual wind makes a person liable for things on his roof. Everyone also agrees an unusual wind makes him exempt. This shows that even רבי מאיר does not make a person pay for a true accident (אונס), so אביי drops רבה's explanation of our משנה. אביי says רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about two moments. During the fall, they argue whether one who stumbles (נתקל) is careless (פושע). After the fall, they argue whether one who gives up his damaging things (מפקיר נזקיו) must pay. The גמרא proves this from the משנה's double wording and applies it to the ברייתא's camel case: the owner stumbled and the camel stumbled over him. רב יוסף and רב אשי explain that רבי יהודה's 'intent' means the owner wants to keep the shards. Finally, רבי אלעזר's statement that the argument is 'at the time of the fall' is read as 'even at the time of the fall,' just like אביי.

steps.title: End of a ruling: exempt in human court, liable before Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The section opens with the end of a ruling begun on the previous page. The person is not forced to pay by a בית דין, but he still owes it in the eyes of Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is exempt according to human laws, but liable according to the laws of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the closing words of a ruling that started on the previous page. The person is exempt in a human court but liable by Heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two levels of responsibility here. A בית דין cannot make him pay. But morally, before Heaven, he should make up the loss. These are the closing words of the חכמים in a ברייתא quoted on the previous page, and the same ברייתא continues in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: exempt under human law; a court cannot force payment
liable under Heavenly law; a moral duty to pay

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'exempt' in court does not mean he did nothing wrong. He still owes it before Heaven.

phrases.english: He is exempt according to human laws,
but liable according to the laws of Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּטוּר מִדִּינֵי אָדָם, וְחַיָּיב בְּדִינֵי שָׁמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ruling from the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Exempt in a human court, liable before Heaven.

steps.title: Both sides agree: usual wind makes him liable, unusual wind makes him exempt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches two cases of agreement. The חכמים agree with רבי מאיר that a person is liable if a usual wind knocks his things off the roof. רבי מאיר agrees with the חכמים that he is exempt if an unusual wind knocks off pitchers he put up to dry.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים agree with רבי מאיר about a stone, knife, or load a person left on top of his roof. If a normal wind knocked it down and it caused damage, he is liable. And רבי מאיר agrees with the חכמים about someone who put pitchers on the roof to dry them. If an unusual wind knocked them down and they caused damage, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא continues with two cases where רבי מאיר and the חכמים agree. The second case shows that רבי מאיר exempts a true accident, which challenges רבה's explanation and sets up אביי's new approach in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal wind is expected, so leaving things on the roof is careless, and everyone says he must pay. An unusual wind is a true accident (אונס), and even רבי מאיר says he is exempt. This shows רבי מאיר never makes someone pay for a real אונס, which undercuts רבה's earlier explanation of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: agree, admit
a usual, normal wind
an unusual, unexpected wind
pitchers, jugs
to dry them

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the line between carelessness and true accident. Even the stricter opinion, רבי מאיר, exempts a real אונס.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי מאיר holds a person liable for everything. This ברייתא proves he exempts a true accident like an unusual wind.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Meir
about his stone, his knife, or his load
that he placed on top of his roof,
and they fell in a usual wind and caused damage,
that he is liable.
And Rabbi Meir agrees with the Rabbis
about one who brings pitchers up onto the roof
in order to dry them,
and they fell in an unusual wind and caused damage,
that he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from step 1. Its last case, where רבי מאיר exempts an unusual wind, challenges רבה's explanation of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר does not hold a person liable for a complete אונס.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about an unusual wind blowing pitchers off a roof.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's explanation of the משנה, which has רבי מאיר making a person pay even in a near-accident case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says רבי מאיר agrees he is exempt when an unusual wind knocks the pitchers down. So רבי מאיר does not make a person pay for a true accident, and רבה's explanation cannot stand.

steps.title: אביי's new approach: they argue about two separate moments
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי מאיר does not make a person pay for a real accident, אביי rejects רבה's explanation. He says רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about two things: damage during the fall, and damage after the fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: they argue about two things. They argue about the time of the fall, and they argue about after the fall.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new way to understand the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה in the משנה. This step only lays out his plan; the details come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא tells us the earlier explanation is dropped. אביי splits the case into two moments. There is the moment the person falls and the jug breaks, and there is the time after, when the pieces and water are lying on the ground. Each moment gets its own argument.

keyTerms.meaning: rather; drops the earlier idea and offers a new one
they argue about two things
at the time of the fall
after the fall

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
They disagree about two things;
phrases.notes: "They" means רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה, the two opinions in the משנה about the broken jug.

phrases.english: they disagree about the time of the fall,
and they disagree about after the fall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised by the ברייתא by replacing רבה's explanation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה: רבי מאיר makes a person pay even in a near-accident case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is really about two separate moments: during the fall and after it.

steps.title: During the fall: is someone who stumbles considered careless?
steps.stepSummary: The first argument is whether stumbling counts as carelessness. One opinion says yes, so he pays for the broken jug's damage. The other says no.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about the time of the fall, in the case of someone who stumbles: is he careless? One master holds that one who stumbles is careless, and the other master holds that one who stumbles is not careless.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains the first of his two arguments, the one about the moment of the fall. The question is whether tripping counts as being careless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If stumbling is carelessness (פושע), the person is to blame for the jug breaking and must pay for damage it causes. That is רבי מאיר's view. If stumbling is not carelessness, he is not to blame. That is רבי יהודה's view. The argument about 'after the fall' will come next.

keyTerms.meaning: one who stumbles or trips
careless, negligent
one master holds

steps.whatToRemember: אביי's first point: רבי מאיר says one who stumbles is careless (פושע). רבי יהודה says one who stumbles is not careless.

phrases.english: They disagree about the time of the fall
about whether one who stumbles is careless.
One master holds: one who stumbles is careless,
phrases.notes: This is רבי מאיר, who makes him pay.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: נִתְקַל לָאו פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא.
phrases.english: and the other master holds: one who stumbles is not careless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of אביי's two-part approach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: one who stumbles is careless (פושע). רבי יהודה: one who stumbles is not careless.

steps.title: The second argument: giving up ownership of the broken pieces
steps.stepSummary: The second argument is about damage after the fall. It depends on whether a person who gives up ownership of his damaging things (מפקיר נזקיו) must still pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about damage after the fall, in the case of one who gives up ownership of his damaging things. One opinion says he must pay. The other opinion says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his explanation by giving the second point that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about: damage that happens after the jug already broke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the jug is broken, the owner does not care about the broken pieces, so it is as if he gave them up. רבי מאיר says he must still pay for damage they cause, and רבי יהודה says he is exempt because they are no longer his. This is a separate question from the stumbling question in step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: After the fall, once the jug is already broken
One who gives up ownership of things that cause damage
One master (opinion) holds

steps.whatToRemember: There are two arguments. During the fall: is stumbling careless? After the fall: must someone pay for damage done by broken pieces he gave up?

phrases.english: They disagree about after the fall
in the case of one who gives up ownership of his damaging things;
phrases.notes: Here that means the broken pieces of the jug, which the owner does not want anymore.

phrases.english: one master holds: one who gives up ownership of his damaging things is liable,
and one master holds: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second half of אביי's two-part explanation, after step 4 gave the first half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the fall the argument is about מפקיר נזקיו: רבי מאיר says liable, רבי יהודה says exempt.

steps.title: Proof from the double wording in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know there are two arguments, and proves it from the two cases in the משנה: slipping in the water and being hurt by the broken pieces.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know this? Because the משנה lists two cases: someone slipped in the water, or was hurt by the broken pieces. But these seem to be the same thing! So the משנה must mean: he slipped in the water at the time of the fall, or he was hurt by the broken pieces after the fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for אביי's idea and proves it from the wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both cases in the משנה were the same kind of damage, there would be no reason to list both. So each case must teach something different. Slipping in the water happens right as the jug breaks, and being hurt by the pieces happens later. That matches אביי's two arguments.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know this?
Slipped
Broken pieces of clay, shards
That is the same as this; why say both?
Rather, is it not so that...

phrases.english: And from where do we know this?
From the fact that it teaches two cases:
phrases.notes: "It" is our משנה about the jug that broke in the public street.

phrases.english: someone slipped in the water,
or was hurt by the broken pieces.
That is the same as this!
Rather, isn't this what it is saying:
someone slipped in the water at the time of the fall,
or was hurt by the broken pieces after the fall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source in the משנה for the two-part explanation from steps 4 and 5.
steps.raayaObject: That the argument covers two separate times: during the fall and after the fall.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's double wording: 'slipped in the water' or 'hurt by the broken pieces'.

steps.title: The ברייתא also has two cases
steps.stepSummary: Since the משנה deals with two cases, the ברייתא must also deal with two cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since the משנה is about two cases, the ברייתא is also about two cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes what it just proved about the משנה and applies it to the ברייתא, setting up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא where רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue lists two cases: a jug that broke and a camel that fell. Just like the משנה, these two cases are read as 'during the fall' and 'after the fall'. This sets up the question of step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
A teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה
Two (cases or things)

phrases.english: And since the משנה is about two cases,
the ברייתא is also about two cases.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא where רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about a broken jug and a fallen camel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the two-case reading proven in the משנה and carries it over to the ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא's argument also covers both during the fall and after the fall.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Comparing it to the משנה, which was just shown to deal with two cases.

steps.title: How can the camel fit the during-the-fall case?
steps.stepSummary: The jug can break during the fall or cause damage after it. The camel works after the fall, when its owner gives up its dead body. But how could a camel's fall be the owner's carelessness?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense with his jug: you can find it either at the time of the fall or after the fall. But his camel: after the fall makes sense, when he gives up ownership of its dead body. But at the time of the fall, how can you find it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the two-case reading of the ברייתא, because the camel does not seem to fit the 'during the fall' case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'during the fall' argument is about whether the person was careless when he stumbled. A person can stumble and drop his jug. But a camel falls on its own, so it is hard to see how its owner was careless. The 'after the fall' case still works, because the owner gives up the dead camel.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense with... (the opening of a question: this part works, but...)
You can find it; there is a real case for it
Its dead body (of the camel)
How?

steps.confusionAlert: The question is only about the camel and only about 'during the fall'. The jug works for both parts, and the camel works fine for 'after the fall'.

phrases.english: It makes sense with his jug:
you can find it either at the time of the fall,
or after the fall.
But his camel:
after the fall makes sense,
you can find it when he gives up ownership of its dead body.
But at the time of the fall,
how can you find it?
phrases.notes: He means: how could a camel falling ever be blamed on its owner's carelessness?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the two-case reading of the ברייתא from step 7 and finds a problem with the camel.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the ברייתא's camel case as covering 'during the fall'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The during-the-fall argument is about a person's carelessness in stumbling. A camel falls on its own, so there seems to be no real case where its owner was careless.

steps.title: רב אחא: the camel crossed a flooded river
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא answers the question from Step 8 by describing a case where the owner led the camel through a river that had overflowed its banks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said: for example, where he led the camel through the overflow of a river.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא tries to answer the question from Step 8: how can a camel's fall be the owner's fault? He says the owner took the camel through a flooded river area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 asked how a camel falling could ever be blamed on its owner. רב אחא's idea is that the owner chose a risky path, through water that spilled over from a river. That choice could make the fall his fault.

keyTerms.meaning: The overflow of a river, where it spills past its banks
For example, such as

phrases.english: Rav Acha said:
For example, where he led it across (through water)
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, 'through water.' The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: by way of the overflow of a river.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 8 about how a camel's fall can be the owner's carelessness.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case definition: describes a specific situation where the owner's choice caused the fall
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A camel's fall seems to have nothing to do with the owner's behavior
steps.terutzMaskana: If the owner took it through a flooded river, the fall may be his fault

steps.title: Either he was clearly careless or he clearly could not help it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אחא: if there was another road, everyone agrees he is careless, and if there was no other road, everyone agrees he could not help it. So there is nothing left to argue about.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If there is another road, he is careless! And if there is no other road, he could not help it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב אחא's case. Either way it is set up, nobody would argue about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is meant to show an argument. But if he had a safer road and chose the river anyway, all agree he is careless (פושע). If he had no other choice, all agree he is not to blame (אנוס). Either way, there is no argument.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How exactly does it look?
Careless, someone who acted wrongly and is to blame
Someone who could not help what happened, so he is not to blame
Another road, a different way to go

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the owner must pay or must not pay. It is saying that רב אחא's case leaves nothing for the two opinions to argue about.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If there is another road,
he is careless!
And if there is no other road,
he could not help it!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי דְּאִיכָּא דַּרְכָּא אַחֲרִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case רב אחא described in Step 9.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dilemma: both possible versions of the case are things everyone agrees on, so neither one can be the case under argument.

steps.title: The owner stumbled and the camel stumbled over him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new case: the owner himself stumbled, and then the camel stumbled because of him. This connects back to the first argument about whether stumbling counts as carelessness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, you find it where he stumbled, and the camel stumbled over him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a better case. The owner tripped first, and then the camel tripped over him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the fall comes from the owner's own stumble, and whether stumbling counts as carelessness is exactly the first argument from Step 4. So the camel can fall because of the owner, and the two opinions can really argue about it.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, which drops the previous answer and gives a new one
You find it, meaning this is the case where it happens
He stumbled, tripped
The camel

steps.whatToRemember: The camel case works because the owner stumbled first and the camel fell over him. That brings it back to the argument over whether stumbling counts as carelessness.

phrases.english: Rather, you find it
where he stumbled,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the owner. He tripped first.

phrases.english: and the camel stumbled over him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב אחא's case after Step 10 showed it does not work.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New case definition that ties the camel to the stumbling argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The camel's fall could only be the owner's fault if he chose a bad road
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner's own stumble caused the camel's fall, so the question is whether stumbling counts as carelessness

steps.title: What does 'intent' mean when he gives up ownership?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the second argument, giving up ownership of damaging things after the fall. It asks how 'intent' could fit that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Giving up ownership of his damaging things: what intent is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the second argument from Step 5. If the argument is about giving up ownership of the broken pieces, what does 'intent' mean?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's view uses the word 'intent' (מתכוין). In a case about giving up ownership after the jug already fell and broke, the fall itself happened without anyone meaning it. So it is hard to see what intention the word could refer to.

keyTerms.meaning: Doing something on purpose, with intent
What is there? Here it means 'what could this possibly mean?'

phrases.english: Giving up ownership of his damaging things:
phrases.notes: This goes back to Step 5, the argument about damage done after the fall.

phrases.english: what intent is there?
phrases.notes: The word 'intent' comes from רבי יהודה's view, which makes the owner pay only when he acted with intent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the stumbling argument to the second argument about giving up ownership, and challenges its wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading רבי יהודה's 'intent' as part of the argument about giving up ownership after the fall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'intent' does not seem to fit a case where the jug has already fallen and broken.

steps.title: Intent means he wants to keep the broken pieces
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף, joined by רב אשי, explains that 'intent' in the case after the fall means the owner plans to keep the shards of the broken jug.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: It is a case where he intends to take ownership of the jug's shards. And רב אשי said the same: it is a case where he intends to take ownership of the shards.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 12 about how 'intent' fits the case of damage after the fall. רב יוסף and רב אשי say 'intent' means the owner wants to keep the broken pieces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner gives up the shards, they are no longer his, so there is no reason to make him pay. But if he plans to keep them, they are still his property, and he can be liable for damage they cause. So 'intent' here means intent to keep the shards, not intent to cause damage.

keyTerms.meaning: he intends, he has in mind
to take ownership of, to acquire
shards, broken pieces of pottery
and so too said (another sage agrees)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'intent' does not mean he wanted to break the jug or hurt anyone. It means he wants to keep the broken pieces as his own.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
It is where he intends to acquire its shards.
phrases.notes: 'Its' means the jug's. He still wants the broken pieces, so they stay his.

phrases.english: And so too Rav Ashi said:
It is where he intends to acquire its shards.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: בְּמִתְכַּוֵּין לִזְכּוֹת בַּחֲרָסֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 12 about what 'intent' means in the case after the fall.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term: 'intent' means intent to keep ownership of the shards.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Intent' seemed to make no sense once the owner gives up the shards after the fall.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Intent' refers to an owner who did not give up the shards and plans to keep them, so they are still his.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: the argument is about the moment of the fall
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the argument in the ברייתא is about damage that happened at the time of the fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: The argument is about the time of the fall.
steps.whatsHappening: A new opinion is brought. רבי אלעזר says the argument is about damage that happens at the moment of falling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא split the case into two parts: damage during the fall and damage after it. רבי אלעזר seems to say the argument is only about the first part. This sets up the גמרא's next question.

keyTerms.meaning: at the time of the fall
an argument, a dispute

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says:
The argument is at the time of the fall.
phrases.notes: He means damage that happens while the jug is falling and breaking, not afterward.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר: בִּשְׁעַת נְפִילָה מַחְלוֹקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new line: instead of explaining each case, רבי אלעזר says where the argument applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument in the ברייתא is about damage at the time of the fall.

steps.title: What about after the fall? Neither answer works
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי אלעזר would say about damage after the fall. If everyone exempts, that goes against רבי מאיר. If everyone makes him pay, that goes against the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: But after the fall, what is the rule? Does everyone agree he is exempt? But there is רבי מאיר, who makes him liable! Rather, what, does everyone agree he is liable? But there are the רבנן, who exempt him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר. If the argument is only during the fall, then after the fall everyone must agree. But we know they do not agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'the argument is only during the fall' means everyone agrees after the fall. But it is already known that רבי מאיר makes him pay after the fall and the רבנן exempt him. So both choices crash, and רבי אלעזר's statement cannot mean 'only during the fall.'

keyTerms.meaning: after the fall
everyone agrees
exempt, does not have to pay
liable, has to pay
but there is (someone who disagrees)

phrases.english: But after the fall, what is the rule?
Does everyone agree he is exempt?
But there is Rabbi Meir, who makes him liable!
Rather, what, does everyone agree he is liable?
But there are the Rabbis, who exempt him!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לְאַחַר נְפִילָה מַאי – דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אלעזר's statement in Step 14 by asking what follows for the case after the fall.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's statement that the argument is at the time of the fall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the argument is only during the fall, everyone must agree after the fall. But רבי מאיר and the רבנן clearly argue after the fall too, so there is no possible 'everyone agrees' answer.

steps.title: It means even at the time of the fall, like אביי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רבי אלעזר: the argument is even at the time of the fall, not only after it. This matches אביי's earlier explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what does 'at the time of the fall' mean? Even at the time of the fall. And he is teaching us the same as אביי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem from Step 15. רבי אלעזר did not mean 'only' during the fall; he meant 'even' during the fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone already knew they argue after the fall. רבי אלעזר adds that they also argue about damage during the fall itself. This is the same point אביי made earlier when he explained the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: even, also
he is teaching us (this new point)
like אביי (in line with his view)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אלעזר, the argument covers both cases: damage after the fall and damage during the fall. 'At the time of the fall' means 'even at the time of the fall,' just as אביי explained.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רבי אלעזר as saying 'only' during the fall. The גמרא just showed that reading cannot work. His point is 'even' during the fall.

phrases.english: Rather, what does 'at the time of the fall' mean?
Even at the time of the fall,
and he is teaching us like Abaye.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי ״בִּשְׁעַת נְפִילָה״ – אַף בִּשְׁעַת נְפִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15 by rereading רבי אלעזר's words.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording: 'at the time of the fall' becomes 'even at the time of the fall.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אלעזר seemed to say the argument is only about damage during the fall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument covers damage after the fall and even during the fall, in line with אביי.
